questions.stem: This bone marrow section from chronic-phase CML most characteristically demonstrates which feature?

explanation.summary: The marrow in chronic-phase CML is moderately to markedly hypercellular, with the fat spaces largely replaced by a proliferating granulocytic (neutrophilic) series and numerous megakaryocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The marrow in chronic-phase CML is moderately to markedly hypercellular, with the fat spaces largely replaced by a proliferating granulocytic (neutrophilic) series and numerous megakaryocytes.

questions.stem: The reciprocal chromosomal event depicted creates a fusion gene whose protein product is best described as what?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An overactive transcription factor driving erythropoiesis

explanation.summary: The diagram shows the t(9;22) translocation moving ABL from chromosome 9 next to BCR on chromosome 22, forming the Philadelphia chromosome. The resulting BCR::ABL fusion encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives the uncontrolled myeloid proliferation of CML.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagram shows the t(9;22) translocation moving ABL from chromosome 9 next to BCR on chromosome 22, forming the Philadelphia chromosome. The resulting BCR::ABL fusion encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives the uncontrolled myeloid proliferation of CML.

questions.stem: In the mechanism shown on the right side of the schematic, the small-molecule agent produces its effect on the receptor by which action?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutralizing the circulating ligand before it binds

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degrading the receptor mRNA in the cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Competitively occupying the extracellular ligand-binding site

explanation.summary: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib bind the intracellular kinase (ATP-binding) domain of the receptor, preventing autophosphorylation and thereby blocking the downstream signal-transduction cascades that drive proliferation. This differs from monoclonal antibodies, which act extracellularly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib bind the intracellular kinase (ATP-binding) domain of the receptor, preventing autophosphorylation and thereby blocking the downstream signal-transduction cascades that drive proliferation. This differs from monoclonal antibodies, which act extracellularly.

questions.stem: This peripheral blood smear is from a patient with polycythemia vera. Which feature best characterizes the appearance shown?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Predominance of blasts containing Auer rods

choices.label: C
choices.text: A crowded field of increased but morphologically normal red cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Numerous teardrop cells with nucleated red cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prominent rouleaux formation on a blue background

explanation.summary: PV smears show a densely packed, crowded field due to erythrocytosis, but the red cells themselves usually retain normal morphology.
explanation.whyCorrect: PV smears show a densely packed, crowded field due to erythrocytosis, but the red cells themselves usually retain normal morphology.

questions.stem: This gross specimen is a markedly enlarged organ removed from a patient with advanced polycythemia vera. What process most likely accounts for the enlargement?

explanation.summary: In the spent phase of PV, bone marrow fibrosis drives compensatory extramedullary hematopoiesis in the spleen and liver, producing massive splenomegaly.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the spent phase of PV, bone marrow fibrosis drives compensatory extramedullary hematopoiesis in the spleen and liver, producing massive splenomegaly.

questions.stem: This schematic contrasts erythropoietin signaling in a normal red-cell precursor with that in polycythemia vera. What is the key molecular abnormality driving the uncontrolled cell growth depicted on the right?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Overexpression of the erythropoietin receptor on the cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of a tumor suppressor gene controlling apoptosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: A JAK2 mutation causing constitutive activation

explanation.summary: Nearly all cases of PV carry an activating JAK2 mutation that keeps the JAK-STAT pathway constitutively active independent of erythropoietin, driving unregulated red cell production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nearly all cases of PV carry an activating JAK2 mutation that keeps the JAK-STAT pathway constitutively active independent of erythropoietin, driving unregulated red cell production.

questions.stem: This normocellular bone marrow biopsy is from a patient with essential thrombocythemia. Proliferation of which cell type is the characteristic finding that accounts for the disease?

explanation.summary: The bone marrow in ET is typically normocellular, but the hallmark is a massive proliferation of enlarged megakaryocytes, often seen in loose clusters throughout the marrow. These are the precursors that spill excess platelets into the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bone marrow in ET is typically normocellular, but the hallmark is a massive proliferation of enlarged megakaryocytes, often seen in loose clusters throughout the marrow. These are the precursors that spill excess platelets into the blood.

questions.stem: This stained bone marrow section from a patient with primary myelofibrosis best demonstrates which underlying pathologic process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Infiltration of the marrow space by sheets of monomorphic lymphoblasts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid macrophages and giant cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replacement of hematopoietic marrow by a dense fibrous meshwork

choices.label: D
choices.text: Diffuse deposition of amorphous eosinophilic amyloid around vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Necrotic gelatinous transformation of marrow fat with serous atrophy

explanation.summary: In primary myelofibrosis the marrow is progressively replaced by fibrous connective tissue (highlighted on reticulin staining), crowding out normal hematopoietic cells and driving extramedullary hematopoiesis and dry-tap aspirates.
explanation.whyCorrect: In primary myelofibrosis the marrow is progressively replaced by fibrous connective tissue (highlighted on reticulin staining), crowding out normal hematopoietic cells and driving extramedullary hematopoiesis and dry-tap aspirates.

questions.stem: This schematic classifies hematologic neoplasms into their major branches, with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) grouped under the myeloid neoplasms. Progression of MDS most commonly leads to which of the related conditions also shown on this classification?

explanation.summary: MDS is a clonal myeloid neoplasm, so it shares a lineage with acute myeloid leukemia; roughly 30% of MDS cases transform into AML. The lymphoid and plasma-cell malignancies shown on the other branches arise from different progenitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: MDS is a clonal myeloid neoplasm, so it shares a lineage with acute myeloid leukemia; roughly 30% of MDS cases transform into AML. The lymphoid and plasma-cell malignancies shown on the other branches arise from different progenitors.

questions.stem: In this peripheral blood smear the central white cell has very few granules and an almost completely clear cytoplasm. This dysplastic granulocyte change is characteristically associated with which condition?

explanation.summary: Hypogranulation and hyposegmentation of neutrophils reflect dysplastic maturation of the myeloid line, a peripheral-blood clue to MDS. Sepsis instead produces toxic granulation (increased, coarse granules), the opposite finding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypogranulation and hyposegmentation of neutrophils reflect dysplastic maturation of the myeloid line, a peripheral-blood clue to MDS. Sepsis instead produces toxic granulation (increased, coarse granules), the opposite finding.

questions.stem: The arrows in this bone marrow field indicate abnormally small cells with single, non-lobulated nuclei. These are dysplastic megakaryocytes; their abnormality would most directly impair production of which blood component?

explanation.summary: Megakaryocytes shed cytoplasmic fragments to form platelets. Dysplastic, small, monolobated megakaryocytes are a marrow feature of MDS and contribute to the thrombocytopenia seen in these patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Megakaryocytes shed cytoplasmic fragments to form platelets. Dysplastic, small, monolobated megakaryocytes are a marrow feature of MDS and contribute to the thrombocytopenia seen in these patients.

questions.stem: This peripheral blood smear is from a patient with acute myeloid leukemia. What morphologic feature best identifies the large arrowed cells as myeloblasts rather than mature leukocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bilobed nucleus filled with bright eosinophilic granules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Abundant granular cytoplasm with a segmented multilobed nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: A small round condensed nucleus with scant clear cytoplasm

choices.label: D
choices.text: A high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio with fine chromatin and visible nucleoli

choices.label: E
choices.text: Densely clumped chromatin with no discernible nucleoli

explanation.summary: Blasts are the earliest, most immature precursor cells. Myeloblasts are large with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, fine (open) chromatin, and prominent nucleoli, distinguishing them from the smaller, mature lymphocyte with its condensed nucleus and scant cytoplasm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blasts are the earliest, most immature precursor cells. Myeloblasts are large with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, fine (open) chromatin, and prominent nucleoli, distinguishing them from the smaller, mature lymphocyte with its condensed nucleus and scant cytoplasm.

questions.stem: The left centrifuged specimen is from a leukemia patient with a WBC count over 600,000/microL; the right is from a healthy donor. What accounts for the markedly expanded middle layer in the patient's sample?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A massive increase in circulating white blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: A large rise in plasma protein concentration

choices.label: D
choices.text: A marked excess of platelets alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: An expansion of the red blood cell mass (polycythemia)

explanation.summary: When centrifuged, blood separates into plasma, a buffy coat of WBCs and platelets, and red cells. Hyperleukocytosis in acute leukemia grossly expands the buffy (WBC/platelet) layer compared with the thin normal band seen in the healthy donor's blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: When centrifuged, blood separates into plasma, a buffy coat of WBCs and platelets, and red cells. Hyperleukocytosis in acute leukemia grossly expands the buffy (WBC/platelet) layer compared with the thin normal band seen in the healthy donor's blood.

questions.stem: This diagram traces the development of every blood cell lineage from a single precursor at the top of the hierarchy. Which property uniquely defines the apex cell shown at the top?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capacity for both self-renewal and differentiation into all blood cell lineages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Terminal differentiation with no further division

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restriction to only the myeloid lineage

explanation.summary: The cell at the top of this hematopoiesis tree is the pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell, defined by its ability to self-renew and to give rise to all myeloid and lymphoid blood elements.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cell at the top of this hematopoiesis tree is the pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell, defined by its ability to self-renew and to give rise to all myeloid and lymphoid blood elements.

questions.stem: The paired diagram and photograph show a large-bore needle being inserted to harvest hematopoietic stem cells. From which anatomical site is this sample most commonly obtained?

explanation.summary: Bone marrow procurement is typically performed under general anesthesia with needles aspirating marrow from both sides of the posterior iliac crest.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bone marrow procurement is typically performed under general anesthesia with needles aspirating marrow from both sides of the posterior iliac crest.

questions.stem: The machine depicted separates circulating stem cells while returning the remaining blood to the donor. What agent is most commonly given beforehand to mobilize these cells into the bloodstream and raise the collection yield?

explanation.summary: Because stem cells are normally scarce in blood, mobilizing agents such as G-CSF (most common) are given prior to apheresis to drive stem cells from the marrow into circulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because stem cells are normally scarce in blood, mobilizing agents such as G-CSF (most common) are given prior to apheresis to drive stem cells from the marrow into circulation.

questions.stem: These intraoral photographs from a transplant recipient show a common regimen-related toxicity. What is the primary cause of this mucosal injury?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bacterial gingivitis from poor oral hygiene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cytotoxic damage from the conditioning regimen

explanation.summary: Oral mucositis (inflammation of the mouth) occurs in most transplant recipients and results from the high-intensity conditioning chemotherapy/radiation given prior to transplant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oral mucositis (inflammation of the mouth) occurs in most transplant recipients and results from the high-intensity conditioning chemotherapy/radiation given prior to transplant.

questions.stem: This chart plots the temporal onset of syndromes complicating marrow transplantation across the post-transplant period. Which complication characteristically appears LATEST, extending well beyond day 100?

explanation.summary: Early complications (mucositis, bacterial infection, acute GVHD) cluster in the first weeks, whereas chronic GVHD is the latest to appear, persisting long after day 100.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early complications (mucositis, bacterial infection, acute GVHD) cluster in the first weeks, whereas chronic GVHD is the latest to appear, persisting long after day 100.

questions.stem: The post-transplant recovery timeline shown distinguishes an early from a late form of one immune complication on the allogeneic track. Around which time point does the transition from acute to chronic graft-versus-host disease conventionally occur?

explanation.summary: Engraftment typically occurs within about 21 days, while acute GVHD gives way to chronic GVHD around day +100, as reflected in the recovery-period timeline.
explanation.whyCorrect: Engraftment typically occurs within about 21 days, while acute GVHD gives way to chronic GVHD around day +100, as reflected in the recovery-period timeline.
